# Craft — Story Structure

How to shape seconds of AI video into something with a beginning, a turn and an ending. Unlabelled content is **[General best practice]**; workflow-proven rules are marked **[Tested]**.

## The unit is the beat

A beat is a moment where something changes for the viewer: new information, a new feeling, a decision, a reveal. Shots serve beats; blocks contain beats.

- One beat = one to three shots.
- One video block (12–20 s, 30 s max) = 2–5 beats [Tested block length].
- Split blocks **at** beats, never mid-moment [Tested].

```text
WEAK    Block 1 ends as she reaches for the door handle; Block 2 opens the door.
STRONG  Block 1 ends after the door swings open on darkness. Block 2 starts with her first step in.
WHY     A block boundary mid-action breaks motion continuity; a finished beat hands off cleanly.
```

## Three rules for short-form [Tested]

1. **Establish the world and the tension in the first 6 seconds.** No slow warm-up.
2. **Build through action, not dialogue.**
3. **End on an image, not an explanation.**

Persona and review content uses its own spine [Tested]: skeptical opener → one specific detail → one honest caveat → considered verdict.

## Hooks (first 1–3 seconds)

| Hook type | What the camera sees | Works for |
|---|---|---|
| In-motion open | Action already happening, mid-gesture | Action, product, UGC |
| Wrong detail | One thing out of place (a door open that should be shut) | Horror, thriller, mystery |
| Direct address | A face at the lens, saying a line with tension | UGC, testimonial |
| Extreme scale | A macro texture or an extreme wide | Product, nature, sci-fi |
| Sound-first | A specific sound before the image resolves | Horror, music video |

```text
WEAK    Opens on a slow pan across the city at sunset to set the mood.
STRONG  Opens mid-sprint: boots hit wet concrete, camera low and tracking, breath loud.
WHY     Motion and stakes in frame one; the world comes along for free.
```

## Beat maps by length

**6 s (one shot or one block):** hook image → turn. A single idea.

**15 s (one block):**
| 0–4 s | 4–8 s | 8–12 s | 12–15 s |
|---|---|---|---|
| Hook / world + tension | Development | Turn / reveal | Image that lands |

**30 s (two blocks of ~15 s):** Block 1 = hook, setup, complication, ending on a turn. Block 2 = escalation, climax, final image.

**60 s (3–4 blocks):** world → disturbance → attempt → reversal → climax → final image. Each block owns one movement of the story and ends on a beat change.

**Teaser / trailer:** world → disturbance → escalation montage → title beat (edit) → stinger.

## Endings

- **Image ending:** the final shot holds long enough to land, usually 3–5 s.
- **Cut-on-the-gasp:** a hard cut at the peak (horror, UGC "stop recording").
- **Echo:** the final image mirrors the first with one thing changed.
- **Withheld reveal:** cut one beat before the full reveal (teasers).

```text
WEAK    She smiles and says, "And that's how I finally found peace."
STRONG  She sets the letter on the fire. It catches. She doesn't watch it burn.
WHY     The image says it; the explanation would undercut it.
```

## Writing the script for video

- Physical actions in [brackets] inline with dialogue, so each line maps onto a video segment [Tested].
- Speaking segments under 8 seconds each [Tested].
- Never write interior states; write behaviour [Tested].
- Dialogue does less work than you think. Prefer a look, an object or an action that carries the information.
- Give each character one concrete physical habit you can reuse across blocks (a ring they twist, a limp on the LEFT leg). It becomes continuity and character at the same time.

## Output format — beat sheet

```
BEAT SHEET — [title] · [total] s · [N] blocks
#  | Time    | Beat            | What the viewer sees                 | Line / key sound
1  | 0–4 s   | Hook            |                                      |
2  | 4–8 s   |                 |                                      |
...
Block split: Block 1 = beats 1–3 (0–15 s) · Block 2 = beats 4–6 (15–30 s)
Ending image: [the exact last frame]
```

## Story checks before the script is handed over

- [ ] The tension is visible by 6 s.
- [ ] Every beat changes something; delete the beats that only repeat.
- [ ] The ending is an image (or a hard cut) with time to land.
- [ ] Block splits fall on beat changes.

# Craft — Directing Performance

AI actors can't take notes, so every performance choice has to be written as visible, physical behaviour with a duration. Unlabelled content is **[General best practice]**; workflow-proven rules are marked **[Tested]**.

## The core rule [Tested]

Physical actions only, never interior states. A video model renders what a camera sees, so give it something to see.

```text
WEAK    She is heartbroken.
STRONG  She reads the text, lowers the phone to her lap, and keeps staring at the dark screen.
WHY     Stillness after an action reads as impact; "heartbroken" is not a pixel.
```

## A vocabulary of visible behaviour

Build emotions from these physical channels instead of naming them.

| Channel | Examples a camera can see |
|---|---|
| Eyes | holds still without blinking · slides LEFT to the door · drops to the floor · unfocused just past the lens · squints against the light |
| Jaw / mouth | tightens · pushes slightly forward · lips press into a line · mouth falls slightly open · swallows |
| Breath | stops · shallow and fast, shoulders rising · one long exhale through the nose · catches |
| Hands | thumb rubs a seam · fingers tap twice then stop · grip whitens on the strap · hand hovers, doesn't touch |
| Posture | shoulders drop · weight shifts to the back foot · leans in an inch · goes completely still |
| Tempo | moves a half-beat slower than normal · stops mid-step · turns too fast |

Combine two channels for a clear read: *"jaw tightens; she doesn't blink"* [Tested phrasing].

## Mechanics that stop the model improvising [Tested]

**Sustained poses need a duration.**
```text
WEAK    He aims the gun at the door.
STRONG  He holds the aim on the door for the full three seconds and does not lower the arm.
WHY     Without a duration the model resolves the pose early.
```

**Involuntary motion needs a mechanism.**
```text
WEAK    He drops the phone.
STRONG  His hand goes limp, the fingers uncurl, the phone slips from a slack grip.
WHY     "Drops" is often rendered as a deliberate throw or toss.
```

**Name the wrong version inline when a mistake is likely.**
```text
STRONG  The glass slips free — she does not open her hand, does not throw it.
WHY     Explicitly ruling out the likely error steers the model away from it.
```

**State sides as hard facts, in capitals** [Tested]: "the cut is above her RIGHT eye", "the bag is on his LEFT shoulder". Models mirror references.

**One action per shot, in sequence.** If a character must do two things, split them across two shots, or chain them with "then" and a beat.

## Dialogue on camera [Tested]

- Dialogue and physical action never overlap. She speaks, or she moves. Sequence it as move → settle → speak.
- Voiceover with no lip sync may play over action shots (hands, inserts, wides with no visible mouth). Label it: `Voiceover, no lip sync: "…"`.
- Leave real silence between lines; write the pause ("she pauses for a full half-second, looking slightly off-lens").
- Give delivery as sound, not emotion: *flat, unhurried, slightly out of breath, half-swallowed last word.*

```text
WEAK    She angrily says, "Get out."
STRONG  She stops wiping the counter. Doesn't look up. Flat and quiet: "Get out."
WHY     Stillness + a delivery note is a performance; "angrily" is a guess.
```

## Voice specification [Tested]

Robotic, synthetic voices are the most common persona failure. Include a voice spec whenever someone speaks, and keep it identical across blocks:

> A natural, warm, human [female/male] voice, casual conversational cadence, real pitch variation, small natural imperfections. Must sound like an actual person, NOT synthetic or robotic.

Adapt the delivery words per character (low energy and dry; clipped and precise; breathless), but never drop the "actual person, NOT synthetic" clause.

## Energy and register

- **UGC / persona** [Tested]: low energy, underselling, talking to the phone like a friend, no smiling at the lens. Understatement reads as credible.
- **Drama:** fewer, smaller movements, longer holds. Stillness is a choice; write it with a duration.
- **Action:** big, clear, single-direction movements; one beat per shot; land each move before the cut.
- **Comedy:** timing is the performance. Write the pause length and the exact reaction shot.

## Blocking and eyelines

- Say where the character is in frame and where they move: "enters frame LEFT, crosses to the window at frame RIGHT, stops".
- Eyelines are hard facts: "@Image1 looks off-camera LEFT toward @Image2". Keep them consistent across shots in a conversation.
- Looking into the lens is a deliberate choice (UGC, confession, horror). Otherwise state "does not look at the camera".

## Performance checks

- [ ] No emotion words; every feeling is a visible behaviour.
- [ ] Every held pose has a duration, and every involuntary motion has a mechanism.
- [ ] No on-camera line overlaps movement, and voiceover is labelled.
- [ ] A voice spec is present and identical across blocks.
- [ ] Sides, eyelines and frame positions are stated.

# Craft — Shot Design and Coverage

Choosing shots that tell the beat, and enough of them to give the edit options. Unlabelled content is **[General best practice]**; workflow-proven rules are marked **[Tested]**.

## Every shot has a job

Before writing a shot, name its job: **establish · reveal · react · detail/insert · move the story · pay off**. If a shot has no job, cut it.

## Shot sizes

| Size | Frame | Use it to |
|---|---|---|
| EWS / extreme wide | figure tiny in the environment | isolation, scale, geography |
| WS / wide | full body plus surroundings | establish space, blocking, entrances |
| MS / medium | waist up | behaviour, gesture, conversation |
| MCU / medium close-up | chest up | dialogue, the default for persona talking heads |
| CU / close-up | face fills the frame | reaction, decision, emotion through behaviour |
| ECU / extreme close-up | eyes, lips, a fingertip | tension, a key detail |
| Insert | an object or hands | product, clue, action mechanics |

## Angles and their effect

| Angle | Effect |
|---|---|
| Eye level | neutral, honest |
| Low angle (camera below eyes) | power, threat, monument |
| High angle (camera above) | vulnerability, surveillance |
| Overhead / top shot | pattern, fate, procedure (hands at work) |
| Dutch tilt | unease. Use it sparingly, once per film at most |
| POV | subjectivity. The viewer becomes the character |
| Over-the-shoulder (OTS) | relationship, conversation geography |
| Propped-phone low and wide | UGC authenticity [Tested] |

## Camera first [Tested]

In every shot description: camera position and movement first, then the subject, then the action, then the atmosphere. Early tokens carry more weight.

```text
WEAK    @Image1 sits on the bed reading a letter, shot in close-up with a slow push.
STRONG  Slow push-in, 50mm, close-up from bedside height. @Image1 sits on the bed, reading the letter.
WHY     The model locks framing and movement first, then fills the frame with action.
```

## Coverage patterns

**Classic scene coverage:** establishing WS → MS of the action → CU of the reaction → insert of the key object → a WS or CU payoff.

**Dialogue:** a master WS → singles for each speaker (MCU) → reaction CUs. Each spoken line in its own shot, with the speaker not moving [Tested rule: dialogue and action never overlap].

**Process / product:** overhead WS → hands insert → macro detail → result shot.

**UGC talking head** [Tested]: selfie MCU at arm's length → propped low-wide → hands-only inserts with voiceover → back to the face for the verdict.

## How many shots per block

- Standard beat: 3–4 s per shot. Travel, reveal or collapse: 5–6 s. Fast cut: 2 s. Under 2 s rarely renders cleanly [Tested].
- So a 15 s block holds about 3–5 shots, and a 20 s block about 4–6.
- Fast micro-cuts (under 2 s each) can sit inside one timestamped segment of at least 2 s as a labelled montage ("three quick cuts: …") [Tested exception].

## Geography and the 180-degree line

- Pick a side of the action and keep the camera on it within a scene. "@Image1 is on frame LEFT, @Image2 on frame RIGHT" as a hard fact in every block of the scene.
- Screen direction: if a character exits frame RIGHT, they enter the next shot from frame LEFT. Write it.
- Crossing the line deliberately (to disorient) is a choice; state it.

```text
WEAK    They argue across the table.
STRONG  @Image1 sits frame LEFT facing RIGHT; @Image2 sits frame RIGHT facing LEFT. Camera stays on the window side of the table.
WHY     Fixed geography stops the model flipping characters between shots.
```

## Composition for the format

- **16:9:** use negative space for tension, put the subject on a third, and use depth layers (foreground object, midground subject, background light).
- **9:16:** stack vertically. Faces sit in the top third, hands and product in the lower middle. Full-body shots read small, so favour MS/MCU and vertical movement (stairs, doorways, tilts).
- Keep the important action away from the frame edges, which platforms crop with UI overlays.

## Output format — shot list

```
SHOT LIST — Block [N] ([start]–[end] s)
#  | Time    | Size/angle      | Lens / move            | Subject + action                 | Job
1  | 0–4 s   | WS, eye level   | 24mm, static           | @Image1 enters frame LEFT         | establish
2  | 4–7 s   | MCU             | 50mm, slow push-in     | @Image1 stops, eyes to the door   | react
...
```

## Shot design checks

- [ ] Every shot has a named job.
- [ ] Shot sizes vary (wide, medium, close) unless sameness is the point.
- [ ] Camera is written first in every shot.
- [ ] Geography, screen direction and eyelines are stated as hard facts.
- [ ] Durations follow the 2 s minimum and total the block exactly.
